lead: Unit 1 fixes the vocabulary of the field: what virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality and extended reality each mean, where they came from, what makes an experience immersive, and what parts every VR system needs. After it you can classify any product as VR, AR or MR, name the hardware and software blocks behind it, and explain why VR must run in real time while ordinary 3D graphics need not.
about: The unit opens with definitions and Milgram's reality–virtuality continuum (1.1), then the milestones that produced today's headsets (1.2). Chapter 1.3 gives the three I's — immersion, interaction and imagination — as the yardstick for judging any experience. Chapter 1.4 separates VR from ordinary 3D computer graphics by its closed real-time loop, and lists the benefits that justify the cost. Chapter 1.5 opens the box: trackers and gloves in, displays and haptics out, plus the computer and the world model. Chapter 1.6 puts VR, AR and MR side by side on the same criteria. Device detail stays thin here; Units 2 and 3 take it up properly.

chapters.idea: VR, AR, MR and XR are four names for four different mixes of real and computer-generated content, with XR as the umbrella over all of them.
chapters.depth: Define VR as a computer-generated, interactive 3D world that replaces the real one and is explored through tracked displays; AR as virtual content laid over a live view of the real world, registered in 3D and interactive in real time (the three tests exams use); MR as real and virtual content combined so a virtual object is anchored to, and hidden by, real geometry; XR as the umbrella term that covers VR, AR and MR. Draw Milgram's reality–virtuality continuum: real environment → AR → augmented virtuality → virtual environment. Some syllabi call the two middle points 'mixed reality' and some call the whole span 'the mixed reality spectrum'. Name the depth ladder non-immersive, semi-immersive, fully immersive, and the term virtual environment for the simulated world itself.

figure.title: Reality–virtuality continuum
figure.aria: A left-to-right line from a fully real environment through augmented reality and augmented virtuality to a fully virtual environment, with AR and VR picked out.

chapters.example: Classify each product and give the reason in one line. (i) A phone shows a 3D sofa standing against your actual wall, and it stays against that wall as you walk around. (ii) A headset shows an aircraft cockpit; your room is not visible at all. (iii) A headset shows your room, and a virtual ball rolls under the real table and vanishes behind its leg. (iv) A phone plays a 360° video that you drag with your finger. Answer: (i) AR — the virtual sofa is registered to real geometry in real time. (ii) VR — the real world is replaced. (iii) MR — virtual content is anchored to the real room and occluded by it. (iv) neither — no tracking and no registration; it is just a panorama on a screen.
chapters.trap: Calling any 3D picture on a phone 'AR', and calling a 360° video 'VR'. Registration with the real world, in 3D, in real time, is the test for AR; a tracked headset that replaces your view is the test for VR.
chapters.leave: How head-mounted displays are built and how AR finds markers or SLAM features go to Unit 3 and Unit 6.

chapters.idea: VR arrived in three waves — early stereo and simulator experiments, the 1980s–90s laboratory era that named it, and the 2010s consumer wave that made it cheap.
chapters.depth: Keep to landmarks that are certain. Wheatstone's stereoscope (1838) showed that two flat pictures can produce depth. Flight trainers from the 1920s–30s put a pilot in a moving mock cockpit. Morton Heilig's Sensorama (patented 1962) combined stereo film, sound, vibration and smell in one booth. Ivan Sutherland's 1965 essay on the 'ultimate display' argued a computer could control matter itself, and his 1968 head-mounted display at Utah hung from the ceiling, hence the nickname Sword of Damocles. VPL Research, founded by Jaron Lanier in the 1980s, built the DataGlove and the EyePhone and popularised the phrase virtual reality. NASA's VIEW system in the late 1980s added gloves and head tracking for astronaut training. The CAVE, a room whose walls are projection screens, appeared in 1992. Nintendo's Virtual Boy (1995) failed commercially. The Oculus Rift Kickstarter in 2012 restarted the field, phone-based viewers followed in 2014, and consumer headsets reached shelves in 2016. Name what each landmark contributed rather than only the date.

figure.aria: A timeline in years with two rows, one for display milestones from Sensorama to consumer headsets, one for interaction milestones, with consumer headsets and inside-out tracking highlighted.

chapters.example: Put these four in chronological order and give the year: CAVE, Oculus Rift Kickstarter, Sutherland head-mounted display, Sensorama. Answer: Sensorama 1962, Sutherland head-mounted display 1968, CAVE 1992, Oculus Rift Kickstarter 2012. Now say in one line what each added: Sensorama added multisensory presentation, Sutherland added head tracking driving a computer-generated view, the CAVE added a room-sized, multi-person view, the Rift added low-cost consumer head tracking with a wide field of view.
chapters.trap: Crediting the wrong person. Sutherland built the first tracked head-mounted display; Lanier's company VPL built the DataGlove and popularised the name; the CAVE came two decades later. Also avoid the claim that VR was invented in the 2010s.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the terms VR and virtual environment.
chapters.leave: How modern trackers measure orientation, and what drift and yaw mean, go to Unit 2; optics and headset display technology go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Any VR experience is judged on three things — immersion, interaction and imagination — and a weak one of the three spoils the whole.
chapters.depth: Define immersion as the feeling of being inside the virtual world: sensory immersion comes from field of view, stereo, resolution, frame rate, latency, spatial sound and haptics; mental immersion comes from story, task and engagement. Say plainly that immersion is a property of the system, while presence is the user's feeling of 'being there' — related but not the same word. Define interaction as the two-way exchange: input the system reads (head and hand tracking, gloves, voice, controllers) and feedback it returns (image, sound, force). Give the real-time demand a number: head tracking that lags by more than about 20 ms between motion and the matching image causes discomfort. Define imagination as the designer's content and the user's mental model — the scenario, the rules, the things that cannot be done in real life (fly a plane, walk through a molecule, rehearse a surgery). Some syllabi write the three I's as 'immersion, interaction, information' — say that the third is usually imagination.

figure.aria: A tree with Three I's at the root and three branches, immersion, interaction and imagination, each splitting into two parts.

chapters.example: A surgical trainer gives the trainee a headset with a 110° field of view and stereo sound, a tracked glove on each hand, and a virtual patient that bleeds when cut. (a) Name the three I's in this system. (b) The head-tracking lag is measured at 100 ms. Which I fails first, and what does the user feel? Answer: (a) immersion — 110° field of view, stereo, stereo sound; interaction — tracked gloves, and the cut that produces a visible and audible response; imagination — the surgical scenario itself, which cannot be rehearsed on a live patient. (b) Interaction fails first: the world arrives late, so the hand and the head disagree, and the user feels dizziness and loses the sense of presence, so immersion collapses too.
chapters.trap: Writing immersion = good graphics. Field of view and latency matter more than polygon count, and mental immersion is not a display property. Keep immersion (system) apart from presence (user).
chapters.leave: The human visual and auditory limits behind these numbers go to Unit 3; interaction techniques and their evaluation go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: 3D computer graphics produces a picture chosen by the animator; VR closes a loop so the picture is chosen by where the user's head and hands are, fast enough to feel immediate.
chapters.depth: Set out the contrast. In 3D computer graphics a scene is built from geometry and a camera path, frames are rendered at whatever time is available, and the viewer is a spectator of a fixed image. In VR the camera pose comes from the tracked user, two images are rendered per frame, one per eye, and the frame must arrive before the user notices — this is the requirement of VR: real-time rendering, stereo, wide field of view, low latency, and tracking in six degrees of freedom. Give the budget: a headset refreshing at 90 Hz allows 1000/90 ≈ 11.1 ms per frame; motion-to-photon latency should stay under roughly 20 ms. Then list benefits: training with no risk and no consumables (fire drill, surgery, machine operation), visualising what is too big, too small, too far or too dangerous (a building before it is built, a molecule, a power grid), remote presence, rehabilitation and pain distraction, education, design review and prototyping that saves money. Close with honest limits: headset cost, cybersickness, missing physical feedback, and content that takes effort to build.

figure.title: The VR closed loop
figure.aria: A downward chain from the user's head movement through trackers, simulation and rendering to the displays, with a dashed edge returning to the user to close the loop.

chapters.example: A headset refreshes at 90 Hz. One frame therefore has 1000/90 ≈ 11.1 ms. In a test, simulation takes 2 ms, rendering takes 7 ms and the tracker-to-display path adds 4 ms. (a) What is the motion-to-photon latency? (b) Does it meet a 20 ms target? (c) What happens at 120 Hz? Answer: (a) 2 + 7 + 4 = 13 ms. (b) Yes, 13 ms < 20 ms. (c) The frame budget falls to 1000/120 ≈ 8.3 ms, so the same 9 ms of simulation plus rendering no longer fits and frames are dropped.
chapters.trap: Describing VR as '3D graphics seen through a headset'. The marks are for the closed real-time loop, the two eyes, and the latency budget — a pre-rendered walkthrough at 5 frames per second is 3D graphics, not VR.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the definition and 1.3 for why latency breaks immersion.
chapters.leave: The rendering pipeline, level of detail, culling and the graphics hardware go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Every VR system is four parts: input devices that sense the user, output devices that stimulate the senses, a computer running the world model and simulation, and the human at the end of both.
chapters.depth: Treat each part at name-and-role level only, because Units 2 and 3 take the devices apart. Input: 3D position trackers (mechanical, magnetic, ultrasonic, optical, inertial), data gloves and gesture input devices, navigation and manipulation interfaces such as 3D mice, joysticks, wands and voice. Output: graphics displays — personal (head-mounted) and large-volume (CAVE, dome, wall) — sound displays, and haptic displays giving force or vibration. Computer and software: the world model or scene database, the simulation engine that applies physics and rules and updates state, the rendering engine, and the VR toolkit or game engine that ties them together; some syllabi call the software half the virtual world generator. The human: visual, auditory and haptic senses set the requirements, so the interface is matched to human limits, not the other way round. Say that head-mounted displays, haptics and tracker internals are covered later.

figure.aria: Four stacked layers of a VR system from the application at the top down to input and output hardware, with the engine and the hardware layers picked out.

chapters.example: A student builds a cheap setup: a ₹1,000 cardboard viewer, a mid-range phone and a Bluetooth gamepad. Name the four components and say which one limits immersion. Answer: output — the phone screen inside the viewer gives the image and the phone speaker gives the sound; input — the phone's inertial sensor tracks head orientation and the gamepad gives button and stick input; computer and software — the phone's processor runs the app and its world model; the human is the fourth part. Limit: the sensor gives only orientation, three degrees of freedom, so leaning forward does not change the view; there is no haptic output and no hand tracking, so immersion stops at looking around.
chapters.trap: Listing only the headset as 'the VR system'. Marks are for all four parts, and the software world model with its simulation engine is the one students forget.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the terms and 1.4 for the closed loop these parts implement.
chapters.leave: Tracker types and their working go to Unit 2; display optics, the human visual system and haptic rendering go to Unit 3; game engines and scene graphs go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: VR, AR and MR differ on three tests: how much of the real world reaches your eye, whether the system knows where the real world is, and whether virtual content is anchored to and hidden by real objects.
chapters.depth: Build a comparison on stated criteria, not on a list of products. Display: VR is opaque and replaces the view; AR is see-through, either optical or by camera pass-through; MR adds depth sensing so virtual objects can be placed behind real ones. Tracking: VR needs only the user's own pose; AR and MR must register the virtual world to the real world, using markers, features or SLAM. Content: VR is fully synthetic, AR overlays on the real view, MR merges both with interaction in three dimensions. Occlusion, interaction, mobility, typical hardware, safety and cost follow. Note that some syllabi place MR inside AR as its advanced form and some place it between AR and VR; write the definition you use and stay consistent. Finish with when to choose which: VR when the real world would only get in the way, AR when the real world is the subject and the user needs free hands, MR when virtual objects must behave as if they were physically present.

figure.aria: A two-circle Venn diagram with the real environment on one side and the virtual environment on the other, and the overlap holding AR overlays and MR anchoring.

chapters.example: Choose VR, AR or MR for each case and justify it in one line. (a) A medical student practises a knee operation and no patient is available. (b) A technician servicing a tractor engine needs both hands free and the manual in view. (c) A shopper checks whether a 2.4 m sofa fits a 2.7 m wall and looks right in the room. Answer: (a) VR — the real world must be replaced so the trainee sees only the anatomy, with tracked tools and no risk. (b) AR — the engine is the subject, the overlay adds the steps, and the hands stay free. (c) AR or MR — the sofa must be registered to the real floor and wall to be measured, and MR if it must also hide correctly behind the real coffee table.
chapters.trap: Writing vague differences such as 'VR is more immersive'. Use the three tests — real world visible, world registration, occlusion and anchoring — and keep your definition of MR consistent all through the answer.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the definitions and 1.5 for the shared components being compared.
chapters.leave: How AR tracks markers and how SLAM works go to Unit 6; see-through display optics go to Unit 3 and Unit 6.
